newsitem.title: USA: U.S. can't let up trade pressure on Japan - Kantor.
newsitem.headline: U.S. can't let up trade pressure on Japan - Kantor.

text.p: The United States has made "good" progress in opening up Japan's markets to foreign goods, but it is still far too early to declare final victory and let up on the pressure, a top U.S. trade official said on Wednesday.
"Let me be adamant about one thing," Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor said. "I don't envisage the day when we can back down from putting bilateral pressure on Japan to open their market."

Speaking to Reuters during the Democratic Party national convention, Kantor also voiced concern about what the United States sees as Japan's intransigence regarding a bilateral agreement to liberalize its lucrative insurance market.
"I'm worried about it," Kantor said. "We reached agreement on October 1, 1994, and frankly it has not been implemented sucessfully."

Japan said on Tuesday that it had given 17 life and non-life insurance companies licenses to do business in each other's turf through subsidiaries. But it was not clear what that meant for the so-called third sector, the tiny slice of the market that U.S. firms dominate and which includes accident and health insurance.
"None of us are quite sure what it means," Kantor said. "We're not sure whether it is trying to implement the agreement or contravening it. You can read it either way."

The United States argues that U.S. companies operating in the third sector should be sheltered from Japanese competition for a while to give them time to penetrate the rest of Japan's newly liberalizing insurance market.

Since President Clinton took office 3-1/2 years ago, the United States and Japan have struck 21 separate trade agreements. Kantor said that insurance was the only one that was not being implemented sucessfully.

"We've made good progress there (in Japan)," Kantor said. "But that's not the end of the story. There are still sectors where we don't have fair access. There will be a need for some more agreements."
He declined to say what sectors those might be.

One area where good progress has been made, according to Kantor, is in the all-important automobile and car parts sector, where the two sides struck an agreement last year after coming to the brink of a trade war. "It's working very well," he said. U.S. automakers though have complained that not
enough Japanese dealers are signing up to sell American cars and have asked the U.S. Trade Representative's office to put Japan on its so-called "watch list" for possible action.

At a joint news conference last year with then Japanese Trade Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto announcing the auto deal, Kantor said the United States expected to have at least 200 Japanese dealerships selling U.S. cars by the end of this year.
Noting that Hashimoto did not contradict him at that time, Kantor said, "It is very difficult not to reach a conclusion that both countries expect (that to happen)."

But Kantor acknowledged that Hashimoto, who is now prime minister, did not commit Japan to that number. The actual agreement between the two sides says the United States should have significantly more car dealerships in Japan.

The Commerce Secretary said there are about 96 such dealerships now in Japan. One reason that there are not more is that one U.S. auto company has trying to get rid of dealerships in poor selling areas to swap them for better locations.
"We just can't let up," Kantor said, summarizing the whole U.S. approach to Japan. "It is the most visible situation to the American public which appears to be unbalanced."
